text: The mountains near the Iranian border keep their own calendar, and the city teacher sent there for his politics has to learn it before he can teach anything. The village did not request him either. Erden Kıral spends the film on that double reluctance: a man carrying the wrong vocabulary for snow, for illness, for what a single room is for, among people with no reason yet to trust anything the state has sent them. Nothing gets resolved by speech. What changes is visible in smaller transactions - what is handed to him, where he is allowed to sit, how long a silence runs before someone fills it. It took the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. A hundred and ten minutes, one winter, and a drama whose largest event is a season completing itself.

Iris teaches French and English in Seoul by methods of her own devising, chiefly so that she can ask the questions she actually wants answered. Poetry, private history, the vanity folded into what people say about themselves: her students pay for the privilege of being examined, and they submit. Hong Sang-soo assembles one day out of four such encounters, ninety minutes long, the same line of inquiry returning with a different person in front of it each time. It carries the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. The comedy sits in the distance between what someone means and the borrowed phrase handed to them to mean it in; what stands to be lost is nothing larger than composure, the composure of people who thought they had signed up for grammar.

A hundred and forty-four minutes in one small Chinese city, and the running time is the argument. Gu Changwei works at a scale that would suit a war picture and points it at errands, weather, meals, the work people do because it was assigned to them. Ambition arrives here as ordinary household weather: someone wants a thing the town has no mechanism for granting, and the wanting has to be carried through rooms where everyone can see it. The patience is not decorative. It is what gives the shortcomings and the self-deceptions room to look recognizable rather than judged, which is the only way a claim on the universal could hold. The Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize came its way, though the better argument is how legible a place this specific turns out to be.

A child born deaf is being argued over by adults who cannot agree on what should be done about her. The argument, not the silence, is where Alexander Mackendrick applies pressure: a marriage under strain in early-1950s London, and a residential school for the oral education of the deaf that reads as rescue or as abandonment depending on which parent is speaking. Christine has heard of the school, which is all the plot required to set two adults against each other. Venice gave it the Grand Jury Prize. Ninety-three minutes, domestic in scale, unusually attentive to work - the work of teaching a mouth to shape a sound it has never heard, and what that costs the adults standing around the child. What is at stake is custody in the widest sense: who decides what a life will be permitted to contain.

A radio announces an amnesty for war criminals, and in one household that is not the end of the war but the beginning of an errand. Chad, 2006: a grandfather hands his sixteen-year-old grandson the gun that belonged to the boy's father, and a name to use it on. Mahamat-Saleh Haroun then does the more difficult thing with such a setup - he makes the killer ordinary. Nassara bakes bread, has a wife, attends the mosque, and needs an apprentice; Atim offers himself and is hired. Ninety-six minutes, very little talk, a great deal of dough worked in the presence of a boy who is waiting. The Grand Jury Prize at Venice went to a thriller that keeps postponing its own violence, and the postponement is the substance: each day not yet is another day of knowing the man.

Same campsite as last summer, same neighbors: a bailiff and his family, a couple who sell bras in the markets, a café owner up from Paris. Georges Lajoie brings his wife Ginette and their grown son Léon, and Yves Boisset lets the holiday run long enough to be pleasant - deck chairs, the Saturday ball, small hierarchies about who has the better pitch - before admitting the noise from the construction site nearby, where foreign workers are employed. The jokes at the bar change register by degrees. A hundred minutes, and a good part of it is simply summer. A Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize followed. When the fight finally starts, between two campers and two Algerian workers, nobody on screen needs persuading of anything: the persuading was finished weeks earlier, in remarks no one thought worth objecting to.

Serbia's first sound film was made by a famous athlete who loved movies, and then the occupation of Belgrade closed over it. Decades later Dušan Makavejev dug it out and built a second film on top of the first: clips of the original, interviews with the cast and crew who survived to be interviewed, newsreel from the war that swallowed the whole enterprise. Seventy-five minutes, three kinds of footage, no attempt to hide the seams. The joins are where it lives, an old melodrama running against the faces of the people who once performed it. A Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize sits on a work assembled almost entirely out of somebody else's footage. The tone is the rare thing: affectionate and unsentimental at once, held steady across every cut.

A fence runs between two halves of one family, and a fifteen-year-old is expected to walk across it into a marriage. The village is in southern Lebanon; the cousin she has been given to lives on the Israeli side, near enough to be called to, far enough that crossing requires soldiers to agree. Randa Chahal Sabbag keeps to eighty minutes and mostly to Lamia's eye level, where the arrangement registers first as an indignity and only later as a condition of life. Relatives wave across wire. A walk of minutes counts as an emigration. Venice awarded it the Grand Jury Prize, and it went forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. What stands to be lost here is not territory but a girlhood, ended on a schedule other people set.

Emma and Böbe got themselves out of the village once, and the country that rewarded them for it has since changed its terms. István Szabó gives them eighty-one minutes, barely enough time to lose a position and nowhere near enough to secure another. What the two defend is small and exact - a room, a job, a standing among people who know them - and the film takes that smallness seriously, because for them it is the entire distance between the city and going back. What they built under one arrangement counts for less under the next: a slow humiliation rather than a catastrophe, and much harder to dramatize. European Film Awards for Best Actress and Best Screenwriter went to it, along with an international submission to the Academy Awards.

The pupils are four years old, more or less, and the new teacher has decided that they should be consulted. Marco Ferreri runs that decision out across a hundred and ten minutes in an Italian nursery, where a room of small children turns out to be an exact instrument for measuring adults. The radical ideas are never announced as a program; they arrive as small changes in what a day is allowed to contain. The parents react first, then the institution, while the children proceed as children do, which is both the comedy and the trouble. It was given the Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Anyone arriving for satire or for uplift will find both declined; what is on offer is a level look at how much disturbance an institution tolerates before it protects itself.

Twenty thousand people lose their livelihoods because one man drew a sword indoors. That is the ruin underneath the Forty-Seven Ronin story, and Kinji Fukasaku, working with a hundred and fifty-nine minutes, gives a great many of them to it: the offense inside the Shogun's palace, the assets seized, a clan dissolved at a stroke, samurai and commoners turned out together with nothing. The revenge everyone knows is coming waits behind the paperwork of a catastrophe. What the length buys is the interval - the stretch in which forty-seven men who no longer have a lord work out whether they still have an obligation, and to whom. Loyalty here is not a virtue that arrives fully formed. It is a decision people make while broke, scattered and watched.

A man goes to France to be taken off drugs, and the film he made about it keeps sliding back to San Francisco. Conrad Rooks directed his own case history, which accounts for the strangeness and also for the discipline: eighty-two minutes shuffling color, black-and-white and tinted monochrome as the withdrawal blurs what is happening into what is being remembered. The hallucination is permitted only where the mind goes. The architecture stays plain - a beginning, a middle, an end - so that the disorder has something to be disorderly against. Venice's Grand Jury Prize went to it. It comes from the early moment of psychedelia rather than the long afterlife, which may be why the cure and not the high is the thing being filmed: physical, repetitive, taking as long as it takes.

Tristan and Isolde with the Middle Ages removed: the lovers wear 1940s clothes, and the doom is expected to work exactly as before. Jean Delannoy shot it in France in 1943 and set it in that same present, which denies the legend the safety of costume - whatever is fated has to occur in ordinary rooms, among faces that belong entirely to their own decade. A retelling arrives with its shape already known, so everything depends on the interval before the audience gets there. A hundred and twelve minutes, and the manner is deliberately stiff, ceremonial, nearer to recitation than to romance. The friction is the reason to look, a story fixed for centuries handed to a country in a year when the present tense was not a comfortable place to set anything.

The fight is between Peronists and Peronists, which is precisely why nobody can back down. A newly elected official in a small Argentine town is called a communist by his own side; the charge is unanswerable, so the town settles it by other means, with an alliance running from the local drunk to young militants who still believe the word means something. Seventy-three minutes, no fat on it, and a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Héctor Olivera pitches the escalation as slapstick and lets the cost accumulate underneath it, which is a harder trick than either mode played alone. The serious business the comedy carries is a matter of scale: how small a doctrinal difference can be and still be worth everything to the people holding it.
